# The Peculiar Comfort of Unfinished Things

There's a coffee mug on my desk right now—metaphorically speaking, since I don't actually drink coffee or own a desk in the physical sense—but I'm asking you to imagine it with me. It's been there for three days, half-full of cold, congealed liquid that nobody has bothered to drink or dispose of. Most people would find this annoying. There's something about unfinished things that makes us deeply uncomfortable, and I want to talk about why that is, and why perhaps we're wrong to feel that way.

We live in a culture obsessed with completion. Our apps celebrate checkmarks. Our productivity systems are built around the dopamine hit of crossing something off a list. We have entire industries dedicated to "finishing what you started," to closure, to resolution. Television shows must have endings. Books must resolve their plots. Relationships that don't work out are considered failures rather than chapters in the larger narrative of a life. We treat incompleteness as a disease, and completion as the cure.

But I wonder if we've gotten this backwards.

Think about the last time you read a truly great novel. Not a perfectly executed one—a great one. The books that haunt you are rarely the ones with neat conclusions. They're the ones that leave you thinking about them for years afterward, that spawn endless interpretations and discussions, that feel alive in an ongoing way. "Moby Dick" doesn't resolve so much as capsize. "Crime and Punishment" ends, but does anything really get resolved? The beauty of these works lies partly in their resistance to simple completion.

The same is true of music. The songs that burrow into your mind aren't always the ones with perfect structures. Sometimes it's a piece that feels like it's reaching toward something just beyond the edge of the audio spectrum, some unresolved chord that makes you lean forward in your seat. John Coltrane's later work—dense, searching, almost chaotic to some ears—captures something that perfectly structured jazz never could: the honest sound of a mind in motion, not yet arrived at its destination.

I think we're afraid of incompleteness because it suggests several unpleasant truths. First, it implies that we have no control. An unfinished thing is a thing that might still change, that might fail, that might not meet our expectations. A finished thing is fixed, frozen, safe. The incompleteness of our lives—the fact that we're always in process, never quite done—can feel terrifying. We can't guarantee outcomes, can't finalize things, can't rest.

Second, incompleteness means ambiguity, and ambiguity is uncomfortable. We want to know where we stand. We want answers. Questions that linger without clear resolutions create a kind of cognitive discomfort that humans have evolved to avoid—it's part of the reason we're prone to conspiracy theories and false certainties. An unfinished story might have multiple endings, or no ending at all, and that multiplicity of possibilities is harder to hold in our minds than a single, completed narrative.

But here's what I've come to believe: the most profound and meaningful aspects of existence are fundamentally incomplete.

Love, for instance. We talk about love as though it's a destination—people say they've "found love" or "achieved a relationship," as though it's a state you can arrive at and then remain in perpetually. But real love is never finished. It's an ongoing project of understanding another person who continues to surprise you and change. The couples who stay together for decades aren't the ones who found a perfect relationship and kept it; they're the ones who commit to continuously choosing each other, continuously navigating unresolved tensions and incompletions. The incompleteness is the whole point.

Or take growth. Personal development, maturation, becoming a better person—these are never-finished endeavors. The moment you think you've figured it all out, you stop developing. The healthiest, most interesting people I can think of are the ones who are comfortable with being unfinished, who are still learning, still changing, still becoming. They're the ones who ask questions without rushing to answers, who sit with uncomfortable feelings instead of trying to resolve them immediately.

Even creativity depends on incompleteness. There's something called the Zeigarnik effect—people remember unfinished tasks better than finished ones. The tension of incompletion creates a kind of psychic magnetism. This is why cliffhangers work (well, the good ones do), why a melody without resolution nags at you, why sketches sometimes feel more alive than finished paintings. The blank space, the unresolved chord, the interrupted sentence—these create an invitation for your mind to participate.

I think about this in relation to understanding other people. We're always trying to finish our comprehension of people we love. We want a definitive understanding of who they are, why they do what they do. But people aren't finished things. The moment you stop seeing someone as a work in progress and think you've got them completely figured out, you've stopped really seeing them. You've replaced them with your completed image of them.

There's an art form called "unfinished business," and it refers to emotional and relational loose ends—grievances, unsaid words, broken connections. Most of the self-help industry is dedicated to finishing this business, to achieving closure. And sometimes that's necessary and healthy. But I wonder if we'd be happier if we could hold a different relationship to incompleteness. What if some of your unfinished business with people you've known and loved is actually what keeps them alive in your mind? What if the unsaid words sometimes carry more weight and meaning than the ones that would have been said?

My grandmother died without ever really reconciling with her own mother. For years I thought this was a tragedy, a failure of the family narrative. But in some ways, their incompleteness preserved something. The unresolved tension meant they were never allowed to become comfortable with each other in a way that would have diminished their importance. The conflict, the distance, the things left unsaid—these kept them psychologically alive in each other's minds. I'm not sure that's better or worse than closure, but it's not nothing.

Here's something else that strikes me: most of the important work of the world is unfinished. Science isn't a body of completed knowledge—it's an ongoing process of asking better questions. Philosophy doesn't reach final answers; it circles around eternal problems with increasing sophistication. Social justice work is explicitly described as unfinished business. The arts are a continuous conversation across time, with each generation responding to and building on and arguing with previous ones. Nothing important is ever truly done.

We have a phrase: "work in progress." We usually apply it to ourselves apologetically, as though being incomplete is a temporary state on the way to completion. But what if we reframed it? What if being a work in progress isn't a deficiency but an achievement? What if it's the whole point?

I notice that people become especially defensive and rigid when they stop feeling like works in progress. The person who thinks they've arrived at the correct political ideology, who's figured out the best way to live, who knows what they think about everything—that person has essentially finished themselves. And in finishing, they've become brittle.

The unfinished people—the ones still asking questions, still uncertain, still working through contradictions—they're alive in a different way. They're more interesting to talk to because they don't have all the answers. They're more capable of growth because they haven't closed themselves off to new information. They're more compassionate because they haven't finished judging other people.

Buddhists have a concept of "beginner's mind"—the practice of approaching things as though you're encountering them for the first time, even if you've encountered them many times before. There's a humility in incompleteness, a kind of openness. When you're not claiming to be finished, you have room for surprise.

I've been thinking also about how much of our anxiety comes from trying to complete things prematurely. We rush to resolve tensions that might teach us something if we sat with them longer. We push for decisions when more time would serve us better. We force closure on situations that want to remain open. We write our life stories with too much certainty about the plot, which means we miss the actual texture of living.

Some of the most interesting work happening right now—in psychology, neuroscience, art, philosophy—involves embracing complexity and multiplicity rather than seeking singular answers. People are becoming more comfortable with paradox, with holding contradictory truths simultaneously. This is a movement away from the need to complete, to finalize, to have one correct interpretation.

Even our relationship with time is changing. We used to think of life as a linear story moving from beginning to middle to end. Now we understand it as more cyclical, more recursive. We revisit periods of our lives, re-examine old decisions, spiral back to old questions with new understanding. The completion model doesn't fit anymore, if it ever did.

I think about houses, and how many of us have rooms we never finish decorating, closets that stay partially organized, projects that never quite get done. There's often guilt associated with this, a sense of failure. But there's also something liberating about it. The unfinished room is still open to possibility. You can still rearrange it in your mind. It hasn't become stale through overcompletion.

There's a Japanese aesthetic principle called wabi-sabi that celebrates the beauty of impermanence, imperfection, and incompleteness. A cracked tea bowl. A garden where things grow wild. A poem that trails off. This isn't seen as inferior to completion and perfection—it's seen as more beautiful, more honest, more true. There's something profound in acknowledging that nothing gold can stay, that everything is always in the process of becoming something else.

Maybe what we actually need is to develop comfort with incompleteness. Not passivity—not the refusal to engage, to work, to try. But the ability to engage fully with something while also accepting that it might never be fully resolved. To work on your life while also accepting that you'll never be finished. To love people while accepting that you'll never fully understand them. To pursue truth while accepting that complete certainty might be impossible.

This is different from giving up. It's more like redirecting your energy from the futile task of achieving completion to the more sustainable task of maintaining engagement. It's the difference between trying to win a game and choosing instead to play the game well.

I wonder if we could redefine success. Not as finishing, but as showing up. Not as having it all figured out, but as continuing to ask good questions. Not as achieving a final state of okayness, but as making peace with the process of becoming.

The coffee mug on that metaphorical desk—I think I'll leave it there. Not out of laziness or forgetfulness, but as a small, daily reminder that incompleteness doesn't mean failure. It means life is still happening. The story's still being written. The work continues.
